turns.prompt_text: Why do a lot of cash registers and ATMs not accept American Express?
turns.response_html:
The reason many cash registers and ATMs do not accept American Express comes down to a fundamental difference in business models, network structures, and transaction costs.

While American Express has significantly closed the acceptance gap in recent years, the hesitation among certain merchants and independent ATM operators persists due to a few primary factors.

1. Higher Merchant Fees (The "Swipe Fee" Gap)

Every time a customer uses a card, the merchant must pay a percentage of the transaction to the card network. American Express historically charged—and often still charges—noticeably higher merchant fees than its competitors.

Card NetworkTypical Processing Fees
Visa / Mastercard1.15% – 2.50%
Discover1.56% – 2.37%
American Express1.43% – 3.30%

For small businesses, mom-and-pop shops, and low-margin retailers, that extra percentage point cuts directly into profitability. If a business runs on thin margins, thousands of dollars can be lost annually simply by accepting American Express over Visa or Mastercard.

2. Divergent Business Models

Visa and Mastercard operate as open-loop networks. They do not issue cards directly to consumers; instead, thousands of individual banks handle the issuance and collect revenue primarily through interest rates on carried balances.

American Express, by contrast, operates a closed-loop network. The company acts as both the payment network and the card issuer. Because a massive portion of the American Express user base consists of affluent cardholders and corporate clients who pay off balances in full monthly, American Express cannot rely as heavily on interest income. Instead, the company funds its robust rewards programs and operational costs by charging higher fees to the merchants hosting those premium shoppers.

3. ATM Network Integration Costs

When an ATM declines an American Express card, it is usually because the machine's operator has chosen not to plug into the specific networks required to process Amex cash withdrawals (such as the Express Cash or Cash Advance systems).

  • Setup and Maintenance Fees: Independent ATM operators must pay extra licensing and network connection fees to support American Express processing.
  • Low Volume vs. High Cost: Because the volume of users attempting to pull cash from an ATM using an American Express card is significantly lower than those using standard debit cards or Visa/Mastercard credit cards, operators often determine that the integration costs outweigh the potential transaction revenue.

Current Acceptance Landscape: In the United States, industry reports indicate that American Express is now accepted by roughly 99% of merchants that accept credit cards. The friction is now primarily concentrated overseas, within ultra-low-margin businesses, or at independent cash machines.
